The '''head cone''' (or '''wax head cone''') is a cone-shaped object shown atop the heads of figures in ancient Egyptian art for well over a thousand years. For most of the modern era it was known '''only''' from paintings and reliefs — no physical example had been excavated — so scholars long debated whether the cones were real objects or a purely artistic convention, like the [[Head Cone|halo]] in later religious art. That debate was settled in 2019. This article gathers the established archaeology, a catalog of '''where the images actually are''', and the deeper interpretation the [[The Library of Ashurbanipal|Library]]'s parent institute has developed — the material a general encyclopedia does not cover.

== The depiction and the long mystery ==

Cone-shaped objects appear on Egyptian heads across roughly '''3,000 BCE to 300 CE''', most densely in the '''New Kingdom''' (c. 1550–1077 BCE), with the first securely dated depictions in the reign of Hatshepsut (18th Dynasty). They sit atop wigs or hair at banquets, festivals, funerals, and offering scenes, worn by women and men, the living and the dead.

Because not a single cone had ever been dug up, a major school of thought held they were '''symbolic only''' — a painter's shorthand for scent, festivity, or blessedness, never actually worn. This is the same reasoning later applied to Christian halos.

== The 2019 Amarna discovery ==

The mystery broke at '''Amarna'''. Excavators recovered cones still in place on two burials — one on the skull of a woman aged 20–29 (found 2010) and a second (2015) — and the analysis was published in the journal '''''Antiquity''''' on '''10 December 2019'''.

The findings overturned older guesses:

* '''Material: beeswax''' — spectroscopy identified a biological wax, '''not''' the fat, resin, or solid unguent long assumed (and still stated by some references). Beeswax was the only biological wax known to the Egyptians.
* '''Structure: hollow shells''' — the cones were not solid lumps of perfume but thin wax shells folded around a brown-black organic core, possibly fabric.
* '''Size:''' roughly 8 cm (about 3 inches) tall.
* '''Context: non-elite''' — the cones came from ordinary workers' burials, not royal tombs, implying '''broad access''' to the technology, not an elite-only rite.

The cones were therefore real, worn objects — and made of wax.

== Where the images are — a catalog of tombs and objects ==

Wikipedia notes only a handful of examples; this catalog collects the principal ones and where to see them, and is meant to grow.

* '''Tomb of [[Head Cone|Nebamun]]''' (c. 1350 BCE, Thebes) — the famous banquet and garden scenes; the surviving fragments are in the '''British Museum'''.
* '''Tomb of Menna''' (TT69, Sheikh Abd el-Qurna, Theban necropolis) — offering and banquet figures wearing cones.
* '''Tomb of Nakht''' (TT52, Theban necropolis) — banquet scene with musicians and guests in cones; one of the best-preserved.
* '''Tomb of Ramose''' (TT55, Theban necropolis) — mourners and banquet figures shown with cones.
* '''Tomb of Ipuy''' (TT217, Deir el-Medina) — daily-life and funerary scenes.
* '''The Amarna burials''' — the two physical cones themselves, from the workers' cemeteries at Amarna.
* '''Painting of Lady Tjepu''' (c. 1390–1353 BCE).
* '''Stele of the priest Renpetmaa''' worshipping Re-Harakhte (c. 900 BCE) — a late example, showing the motif's persistence.
* '''New Kingdom banquet and dancer scenes''' (c. 1400 BCE) — musicians and dancers in cones recur across the Theban tombs.

''(This is an initial catalog. Adding tombs, TT numbers, and current museum locations is exactly the kind of "where Wikipedia is lacking" contribution the Library wants.)''

== Mainstream interpretations ==

Egyptology's leading readings, not mutually exclusive:

* '''Perfume / unguent cone''' — the cone melts with body heat and spreads scent; the dominant textbook explanation.
* '''Festival &amp; banquet marker''' — worn at feasts and celebrations, signalling a state of enjoyment or honour.
* '''Fertility / rebirth symbolism''' — links to Hathor, sensuality, and regeneration.
* '''Funerary / afterlife''' — worn by the deceased to signal transfiguration and the blessed state.

== The Van Kush Family Research Institute reading (proposed) ==

'''Attribution note:''' the following is the original interpretation of '''Rev. Ryan Van Kush''' and the '''Van Kush Family Research Institute (VKFRI)''', developed through research and hands-on saponification (soap- and candle-making) practice. It is '''presented as the Institute's hypothesis, not established Egyptology'''; several points (below) diverge from or are rejected by the mainstream, and are flagged as such. It is included because it is the deep, connective material the Library exists to hold.

VKFRI proposes that the head cone is one node in a much larger '''wax technology''' — pharmaceutical, ritual, and consciousness-preserving — that runs from Egypt through the Phoenician and Biblical worlds into later art:

* '''A sun-melting ritual.''' Sun-disks in tomb paintings are shaded '''identically''' to the cones and garments, which VKFRI reads as evidence of a deliberate '''sun ritual''': in summer heat the wax melts, running down wig, shoulders, and sheer linen to create a visible sunrise/sunset glow. (VKFRI's own observation.)
* '''Kyphi as the filling.''' The cone's melting mixture is identified as '''[[Kyphi]]''' — the Egyptian incense-perfume-medicine (raisins, wine, honey, frankincense, myrrh, mastic, pine, cinnamon/cardamom). Cinnamon warms (aids the "melting" sensation), is antiseptic, and promotes circulation — enhancing '''transdermal''' absorption through the sheer linen.
* '''Sheer linen as a delivery system.''' Translucent Egyptian linen is read not as mere fashion but as a '''transdermal pharmaceutical layer''' for the melting wax-Kyphi.
* '''Head cones as the origin of the halo.''' The luminous melted-wax effect in lamplight is proposed as the '''literal origin''' of the later glow/halo — Egyptian cone → Fayum → early Christian light → Byzantine gold halo.
* '''The "T" hieroglyph as wax''' (contested). VKFRI proposes the sign traditionally read as a "loaf of bread" (Gardiner X1) is actually '''saponified beeswax''' — noting the long-standing anomaly that the sign is coloured black or blue (Nile-flood colours, not bread) and sometimes shown with running water (soap). ''Mainstream Egyptology reads X1 as bread; this is a VKFRI proposal.''
* '''Punic Wax &amp; the Phoenician thread.''' Links the cone to '''Punic wax''' (''cera punica'', saponified beeswax described by Pliny), Mount Hermon and the "dew of Hermon" of '''Psalm 133''', the Fayum mummy portraits, and encaustic painting — a continuous "wax consciousness" lineage (the "'''Zar thread'''"). ''The "sine cera" = "without wax" etymology of "sincere" cited here is folk etymology, rejected by most linguists — VKFRI cites it for cultural significance, not as fact.''
* '''An initiation / midwife rite.''' The summer feast (August) and the non-elite Amarna burials are read as a '''democratized medical-spiritual initiation''' (e.g. women entering healing/midwifery), the cone marking new status.

Where these proposals touch verifiable ground — the 2019 beeswax finding, Kyphi's ingredients, Punic wax, Psalm 133's text, encaustic technique — the article cites it; where they are the Institute's own synthesis, they are marked "VKFRI proposes."
